newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durable goods orders rebound, growth moderate.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durable goods orders rebound, growth moderate.

text.p: A rebound in orders for durable goods in June, led by transportation equipment, suggested the U.S. economy remains within the boundaries of moderate growth, economists said.
Orders rose 2.3 percent in June, their biggest jump since January. And, while the number surpassed forecasts for a 1.4 percent rise, experts conceded the report held no surprises.
"Orders have been basically strong all year and this report basically confirms that trend," said James Padinha, an economist at Briefing.Com.

Some analysts forecasted large volume aircraft orders from Boeing Co in the past several months would lift the overall number to as high as 5.0 percent. Those orders have trickled into the data, but without them economists said an ex-aircraft rise of 1.7 percent and ex-transportation rise of 0.8 percent were sound assurances of a mild growth rate.

"Most people were looking only for a small gain in ex-transportation, but we got an increase ... that's 3/4 of a percentage point above expectations," said Cary Leahey, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics.

The rise in durables portends a beefier third quarter gross domestic product than the two to 2-1/2 percent growth seen for Q2, analysts said. But again, they stressed it would be "healthy" growth not reflective of an overheating economy.
Year-on-year durable goods growth now stands between five and six percent, Padinha said, faster than that seen in 1996.

The number is also consistent with other recent gains associated with manufacturing -- such as higher industrial production and a longer manufacturing workweek. Perhaps the most salient point, Padinha said, is that these numbers have yet to manifest themselves on the demand side.

"This stuff is out there for people to buy and it stands to reason that a lot of durable goods components will find demand, especially considering the rise in house sales we've seen," Padinha said. "So this is more of a going forward type thing supporting buying."

Conversely, in an abrupt turnaround, electrical machinery orders in June were flat compared with a 10.7 percent jump in May and a 10 percent rise in April, the government said. And industrial machinery orders remained soft, declining 0.6 percent in June compared with a 3.1 percent drop in May.
"Most people are comfortable with moderate growth and this is a report that is consistent with that," said Dan Seto, senior economist at The Nikko Securities Co International Inc.

Padinha said some acceleration already was expected and there would be no significant revisions of GDP estimates. In the same vein, he said the Federal Reserve was unlikely to rethink its current take on moderate economic growth.
Fed policymakers will need to view durable goods reports for at least a couple of months together before the data would have much impact, other economists said.
